title: The Great Dosa Debate: Fork and Spoon, or Tear It With Your Hands?
excerpt: A viral video reignites the eternal argument over how to eat India's beloved crepe — and diaspora Indians have strong opinions
body:
• Viral videos of Indian food being eaten with cutlery have repeatedly sparked fierce online debates about cultural authenticity and dining traditions
  • Comedian Saikiran's reel dividing masala dosa eaters into "centre" and "side" camps racked up massive engagement, with the fork-and-knife approach dismissed as a betrayal of the dish
  • Ayurvedic tradition links eating with hands to mindful digestion, and chefs say the tactile experience of tearing crisp dosa is integral to enjoying it
  • For diaspora Indians navigating Western dining norms, the dosa question touches something deeper: how much of your food culture do you adapt, and how much do you defend?

A Crispy Controversy

Few foods test the boundaries of Indian dining etiquette quite like the dosa. A paper-thin rice-and-lentil crepe the size of a forearm, stuffed with spiced potato, flanked by coconut chutney and sambar — the masala dosa was never designed for polite Western cutlery. And yet, every few months, someone on social media tries to eat one with a fork and spoon, and the internet loses its collective mind.

The latest flare-up follows a pattern that has become almost ritualistic. Hyderabad-based comedian Saikiran posted a reel dissecting the two tribes of masala dosa eaters: the "centre eaters" who plunge straight into the potato-filled middle, and the "side eaters" who tear from the crispy edges inward. His verdict was emphatic. The fork-and-knife approach, popularised by food vloggers, was a "fork and knife moment" — code for trying too hard. The real way to eat a masala dosa, he argued, is to tear it from the side, dunk it in chutney or sambar, and work your way to the center, where the hot potato filling keeps everything warm.

"If you begin in the middle and then reach the edges, it will lose its crispness. It's a race against time in air-conditioned restaurants."

— Saikiran, comedian, on why side-eating is the superior strategy

Cutlery as Culture War

The dosa debate is just one front in a larger reckoning over Indian food and Western dining norms. In October 2025, a UK-based "samosa specialist" posted a video titled "Samosa eating etiquette," carefully slicing into a samosa with a knife and fork while dipping each piece into chutney with surgical precision. The clip, shared on X by @JeetN25, crossed 684,000 views and triggered an avalanche of mockery.

"Can we just stop teaching ourselves British table etiquette and try eating Indian food the way it is supposed to be eaten?" one user wrote. Another summed it up with characteristic bluntness: "Kaise kaise log hain yaar."

The pushback goes beyond humor. When New York politician Zohran Mamdani was filmed eating rice with his hands during the 2025 mayoral race, US Congressman Brandon Gill told him to "go back to the Third World." The moment crystallised what many diaspora Indians already felt: that the simple act of eating with your hands — something billions of people do daily — can still be weaponised as a marker of backwardness in Western spaces.

The Ayurvedic Case for Hands

There is a rich cultural logic behind eating with your hands that predates the fork by millennia. In Ayurvedic tradition, each finger represents one of the five elements — earth, water, fire, air, and ether. The act of touching food before it enters the mouth is believed to align these elements and signal the digestive system to prepare.

Chef Stanley Coelho of Moxy Bengaluru puts it in more sensory terms. "Eating with your hands heightens the experience — it engages more than just taste, allowing texture, temperature, and aroma to play their part," he told Tasting Table. "Tear small pieces, fold them neatly, and you'll enjoy both the flavor and the ritual without the mess."

As one commentator put it in an essay for OBNews: "If you've eaten a masala dosa with a knife and fork, you already know — humility isn't the first word that comes to mind. Humiliation might be."

The Diaspora Dilemma

For Indians living abroad, the dosa question is never purely about the dosa. It is about navigating a world where your grandmother's way of eating is treated as uncouth at business dinners, while the same cuisine earns Michelin stars across Manhattan and London. Indian restaurants are being celebrated globally — chefs curating regional thalis and fermented pickles with great flourish — but the moment a diner eats the food the way it was designed to be eaten, eyebrows go up.

The social media debates reflect this tension. Many diaspora Indians confess to code-switching at the table: hands at home, fork and knife at restaurants, a careful negotiation between authenticity and assimilation. The dosa, with its unwieldy size and impossible-to-cut crispness, resists that compromise. You either tear it or you fight it.

"Culture is defined by the depth of your connection to food, not the length of your cutlery."

— OBNews commentary on the Indian food etiquette debate

No Wrong Way, But Maybe a Better One

Not everyone is absolutist. Etiquette author Sana Grover, who wrote "The Glow Up Guide," takes a more pragmatic view. Context matters — formal settings might call for cutlery, but casual meals with family should honor tradition. The real faux pas, she and Chef Coelho agree, is not whether you use a fork, but whether you waste food on your plate or start eating before the elders at the table.

Still, there is something about the dosa that resists modernity's cutlery. Its shape demands tearing. Its crispness rewards speed. Its accompaniments — the soupy sambar, the gritty chutney — work best when scooped with a torn piece rather than balanced on metal tines. The dosa is, in every sense, a hand food.

And if the internet has proven anything, it is that Indians worldwide will defend that truth with an enthusiasm that borders on the sacred. Fork and knife? Keep it for the steak. The dosa knows what it wants.
nri_angle: Explores how diaspora Indians navigate the tension between traditional hand-eating culture and Western dining norms, using the dosa as a lens for the broader code-switching experience at the table
